source_text: Sic autem infirmitas humana sese habet, ut, cum mortuum in somnis quisque uiderit, ipsius animam se uidere arbitretur, cum autem uiuum similiter somniauerit, non eius animam neque corpus, sed hominis similitudinem sibi adparuisse non dubitet. quasi non possint et mortuorum hominum eodem modo nescientium non animae, sed similitudines adparere dormientibus. pro certo, cum Mediolani essemus, audiuimus, quod cum debitum repeteretur a quodam defuncti patris cautione prolata, quod filio nesciente a patre iam fuerat persolutum, contristari homo grauissime coepit atque mirari. quod ei pater moriens non dixerit, quid deberet, cum fecisset etiam testamentum. tunc ei nimis anxio adparuit idem pater eius in somnis et ubi esset recautum, quo illa cautio uacuata fuerat, indicauit. quo inuento iuuenis atque monstrato non solum falsi debiti calumniam propulsauit, sed etiam paternum recepit chirographum, quod pater non receperat, quando est pecunia persoluta. hic utique putatur anima hominis curam gessisse pro filio et ad eum uenisse dormientem, ut docens. quod ignorabat, magna molestia liberaret. sed eodem ipso ferme tempore, quo id audiuimus, id est nobis apud Mediolanum constitutis Carthaginis rhetor Eulogius, qui meus in eadem arte discipulus fuit, sicut mihi ipse, posteaquam in Africam remeauimus, retulit, cum rhetoricos Ciceronis libros discipulis suis traderet, recensens lectionem, quam postridie fuerat traditurus, quendam locum offendit obscurum, quo non intellecto uix potuit dormire sollicitus. qua nocte somnianti ego illi quod non intellegebat exposui, immo non ego, sed imago mea nesciente me et tam longe trans mare aliquid aliud siue agente siue somniante et nihil de illius curis omnino curante. quomodo fiant ista nescio; sed quomodolibet fiant. cur non eodem modo fieri credimus, ut in somnis quisque uideat mortuum, quomodo fit, ut uideat et uiuum? ambobus utique nescientibus neque curantibus, quis uel ubi uel quando eorum imagines somniet.
thought_title: Dream-images of the dead are like dream-images of the living
orientation: Augustine is arguing that appearances of the dead in dreams are likenesses, not the dead person's soul, just as dreams of living people are likenesses.
pass_a_gloss: But human weakness is such that, when anyone sees a dead person in dreams, he thinks he sees the soul itself of that person, but when he has similarly dreamed of a living person, he does not doubt that not the soul nor the body of that person, but a likeness of the person has appeared to him. As if likenesses of dead people also, who in the same way do not know, could not appear to sleepers, not souls but likenesses. For certain, when we were at Milan, we heard that when a debt was being demanded from a certain man with the bond of his deceased father produced, which had already been paid by the father without the son knowing, the man began to be very gravely distressed and to wonder. Because his dying father had not told him what he owed, although he had even made a will. Then to him, exceedingly anxious, his same father appeared in dreams and showed where the receipt was, by which that bond had been voided. When the young man had found and shown this, he not only drove off the false accusation of a debt, but also received back his father's written bond, which the father had not received back when the money was paid. Here certainly the soul of the man is thought to have taken care for his son and to have come to him sleeping, so that by teaching what he did not know, it might free him from great trouble. But at almost that same time at which we heard this, that is while we were staying at Milan, Eulogius the rhetor of Carthage, who was my student in that same art, as he himself reported to me after we returned to Africa, when he was delivering the rhetorical books of Cicero to his students, reviewing the reading which he was going to deliver on the next day, he came upon a certain obscure passage, and not understanding it he could scarcely sleep for worry. On that night, while he was dreaming, I explained to him what he did not understand; no, not I, but my image, without me knowing and so far away across the sea doing something else or dreaming something else and caring nothing at all about his concerns. How these things happen I do not know; but however they happen, why do we not believe that it happens in the same way that anyone sees a dead person in dreams, as it happens that he sees also a living person? Both certainly not knowing and not caring who or where or when dreams their images.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'likeness' for similitudo, and Augustine is contrasting likeness with the actual soul or body.
A cautio is a written obligation or bond for a debt; 'bond' is the standard legal sense.
Recautum is a counter-document showing the debt was paid; 'receipt' captures the function.
Chirographum is a handwritten document of debt; 'written bond' preserves the handwritten and debt aspects.
Calumnia here is a false claim of debt; 'false accusation' captures the legal wrong.
Augustine explicitly says 'not I, but my image' (imago mea), and 'image' is the natural English for imago.

pass_b_english: Human weakness is such that when someone sees a dead person in a dream, he thinks he is seeing that person's soul; but when he dreams of a living person in the same way, he does not doubt that what appeared to him was not that person's soul or body but a likeness of the person. As if the likenesses of dead people—who likewise know nothing—could not appear to sleepers in the same way. For certain, when we were in Milan, we heard that a debt was being demanded from a man on the strength of a bond produced by his deceased father, a bond the father had already paid off without the son's knowledge. The man began to be deeply distressed and astonished that his father had not told him as he was dying what he owed, since he had even made a will. Then, in his great anxiety, his father appeared to him in a dream and showed him where the receipt was that had cancelled that bond. When the young man found it and produced it, he not only drove off the false accusation of an unpaid debt but also recovered his father's written bond, which his father had not received back when the money was paid. Here one would certainly think that the man's soul had taken care for his son and had come to him while he slept, so that by teaching him what he did not know, it might free him from great trouble. But at almost the same time that we heard this—that is, while we were staying in Milan—Eulogius, a rhetorician of Carthage who had been my student in that art, as he himself told me after we returned to Africa, was lecturing his students on Cicero's rhetorical books. While reviewing the lesson he was to give the next day, he came upon an obscure passage, and because he could not understand it he could hardly sleep for worry. That night, as he dreamed, I explained to him what he did not understand—or rather, not I, but my image, while I knew nothing of it and was far away across the sea, doing or dreaming something else and not caring at all about his concerns. How these things happen I do not know; but however they happen, why do we not believe that a person sees a dead man in dreams in the same way that he sees a living one? In both cases, surely, the people themselves neither know nor care who dreams their likenesses, or where, or when.

dismissed.why: The English omits "anima hominis" (the soul of the man/his soul). The whole point is that people THINK it's the soul, but Augustine argues it's only an image. Missing "soul" weakens the contrast with "image" later.
dismissed.note: The English already says 'that the man's soul had taken care'; the checker quoted only part of the sentence.
